subject: zoology
question_text: What is the class to which the flukes belong? Write short notes on the chief characters of that group.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.64, SAQ 180). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. BOOK IMPRECISION: the book's point 6 says flukes are 'bisexual' (its word for hermaphrodite) and its point 9 names Schistosoma as an example on the same page. Schistosoma is unisexual, so the two points contradict each other. The card states the general rule and names the exception, and the book's wording is recorded in that step's `why`.

steps.label: The class
steps.why: The question asks for the class first, so the name Trematoda and its phylum are written before any character of the group.
common_mistakes: Writing Cestoda. Cestoda is the class of the tapeworms; the flukes are Trematoda.
Naming the phylum Nematoda. Flukes are flatworms, phylum Platyhelminthes.
steps.memory_tip: Trematoda for the flukes, Cestoda for the tapeworms, Turbellaria for the free-living flatworms.
steps.margin_note: Class and phylum in the first line. That is the first mark.

steps.label: Body and suckers
steps.why: A parasite in a moving gut or a flowing blood vessel has to stay in place, so the suckers and the protective tegument are the two features every fluke shows.
common_mistakes: Calling the covering a cuticle. In a fluke it is a living tegument.
Naming only one sucker. The oral sucker and the ventral acetabulum are both expected.
steps.memory_tip: Two suckers: one at the mouth, one on the belly, and that one is the acetabulum.
steps.margin_note: Covering, then the two suckers by name. Five or six lines.

steps.label: Gut and reproduction
steps.why: A forked blind gut carries the food to both sides of a flat body, so no circulatory system is needed to distribute it. BOOK NOTE: the source book lists flukes flatly as 'bisexual' and names Schistosoma as an example on the same page; Schistosoma is unisexual, so this card states the general rule and the exception.
common_mistakes: Giving the fluke an anus. The gut is blind; the waste leaves by the mouth.
Writing that every fluke is hermaphrodite. Schistosoma has separate sexes.
steps.memory_tip: A forked blind gut, and one body with both sets of organs — except in Schistosoma.
steps.margin_note: Gut in two lines, reproduction in two. Name the exception if there is room.

steps.label: Life cycle and examples
steps.why: Each larval stage multiplies in number inside the intermediate host, which is why a fluke with a two-host life cycle can still reach a new final host.
common_mistakes: Giving the larval stages in the wrong order. It runs miracidium, sporocyst, redia, cercaria.
Writing that the fluke needs one host only. There is more than one host in the life history.
steps.memory_tip: Miracidium, sporocyst, redia, cercaria — four stages, in that order, inside the snail.
steps.margin_note: The list of larval stages is the marked part. Keep it in order, then close with the examples.
